articles.title: Turtle Herbivory Suppresses Seagrass Function but Reveals Recovery Potential in a Remote Coral Reef Atoll

articles.title: An integrated GIS and remote-sensing framework for district-level dengue risk assessment in northern India: development of a spatial Dengue Risk Index and assessment of its spatial concordance with reported incidence
paragraphs: Dengue is an increasingly important vector-borne disease driven by climate variability, urbanization, environmental change, and population growth. Despite its rising burden in northern India, district-level spatial epidemiological frameworks integrating environmental suitability, transmission hazard, and population vulnerability remain limited. This study developed an integrated geographic information system (GIS)- and remote-sensing (RS)-based Dengue Risk Index (DRI) describing long-term spatial susceptibility to dengue in Gorakhpur district, Uttar Pradesh, and assessed its spatial concordance with reported dengue incidence.

A GIS-based multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) framework incorporating the analytic hierarchy process (AHP) integrated 14 environmental, topographic, hydrological, and socio-demographic variables into three thematic components: the Environmental Suitability Index (ESI; six variables), Hazard Index (HI; five variables), and Vulnerability Index (VI; three variables). Relative humidity and the Normalized Difference Moisture Index were excluded after redundancy screening. Rainfall was derived from India Meteorological Department (IMD) 0.25° daily gridded data for 2025, elevation from the Copernicus 30 m DEM, and population density from WorldPop 2025 constrained estimates. Standardized (1–5) raster layers were integrated using the Weighted Linear Combination (WLC) approach to construct the DRI. Spatial concordance between block-level mean DRI and laboratory-confirmed dengue incidence in 2025 (225 cases, 20 blocks) was assessed using Pearson’s and Spearman’s correlation, linear and negative binomial regression, influence diagnostics, and global Moran’s I with Lagrange multiplier tests for spatial dependence.

The DRI (1–5 relative scale) showed marked spatial heterogeneity, with higher values in the central and western parts of the district. Chargawan, which contains Gorakhpur city, was the only block classified as Very High risk, followed by Sahjanwa, Piprauli, and Jungle Kaudia (High), whereas Brahmpur was classified as Very Low risk. Overall, 32.87% of the district (1,090.2 km2) was classified as High or Very High risk. The single very high-risk block accounted for 48.9% of reported cases. However, concordance between block-level DRI and incidence was weak and not statistically significant (Pearson's r = 0.16, p = 0.49; Spearman's ρ = −0.003, p = 0.99; R2 = 0.03; incidence rate ratio per 0.1 DRI = 1.05, 95% CI 0.91–1.21). Neither incidence nor the regression residuals showed significant spatial autocorrelation (Moran's I = −0.13 and −0.17; p ≥ 0.44), so spatial regression was not required.

The DRI provides a transparent, reproducible description of long-term spatial susceptibility to dengue that integrates environmental suitability, transmission hazard, and population vulnerability. Because its concordance with single-year, block-level incidence was weak and non-significant, it should not be interpreted as a predictor of dengue incidence or as a validated risk model. The framework may help district programs structure surveillance planning, but multi-year incidence, finer spatial units, and entomological data are needed before it is used to allocate interventions.

articles.title: Analytical Approaches for Detection, Characterization, and Environmental Significance of Suspended Particulate Matter in Aquatic Systems: A Scoping Review
paragraphs: Suspended particulate matter (SPM) represents a component of aquatic systems, acting both as a carrier of contaminants and as a factor shaping ecosystem functioning. This review summarizes recent progress in methods for detecting and quantifying SPM in natural waters. Traditional gravimetric analysis provides a direct mass‐based reference, while optical approaches such as turbidimetry and nephelometry enable rapid and automated assessments. Granulometric techniques, including sedimentation and laser diffraction, contribute to understanding particle size distribution and its role in transport, settling, and pollutant interactions. Chemical characterization, based on spectroscopic and spectrometric methods, identifies the composition of SPM and its association with heavy metals, organic pollutants, and microplastics. Particular attention is given to the ecological risks posed by fine particles, which remain suspended longer and enhance contaminant mobility. The review integrates findings from hydrochemistry, analytical chemistry, and environmental monitoring, outlining both the strengths and limitations of existing methods and highlighting directions for improving water‐quality assessment and ecological risk evaluation.

articles.title: Inkjet and Related Printing Technologies for Plant Systems: From Physiological Monitoring to Functional Biofabrication
paragraphs: Featuring non-contact, high-precision, and multi-material deposition, inkjet and related printing technologies offer a new alternative technique for plant systems. However, the spatial heterogeneity, continuous growth, and sensitivity of plant tissues to external perturbations make it difficult for conventional methods to target specific sites on living organs. This review evaluates thermal and piezoelectric inkjet printing, together with aerosol jet and electrohydrodynamic printing for plant applications. Moreover, it relates the jetting behavior of the printhead to interfacial processes between droplets and plant surfaces. Practical performance is assessed across four dimensions: effective feature size, organ-scale throughput, potential biological damage, and the physiological compatibility of printing inks with plants. Applications are then organized within a framework comprising five tiers: monitoring, delivery, sensing, biofabrication, and intelligent systems. Specifically, recent studies have demonstrated that these printing approaches can be employed for surface labeling and growth tracking of plant organs, localized delivery of agricultural inputs, fabrication of flexible sensors, and construction of living materials (e.g., plant cells). Combined with artificial intelligence technology, these capabilities could form a closed-loop system spanning sensing to feedback, with printing as the precision actuator, potentially shifting plant management from passive observation to active regulation. Finally, this review discusses the challenges of living-interface dynamics, ink biocompatibility, multiscale integration, and data intelligence. It further outlines the prospects of these technologies for programmable plants and living agricultural interfaces. By bridging printing technologies, plant systems, and functional biofabrication, this review provides a unified framework to guide the development of intelligent and sustainable agricultural systems.

articles.title: Differential Impacts of Anthropogenic Disturbance on Community Composition and Alpha Diversity of Macroinvertebrates at a Large Urban River System
paragraphs: Macroinvertebrates play critical roles in aquatic ecosystems, yet the effects of anthropogenic land‐use disturbance on macroinvertebrate communities and their taxonomic and functional diversity remain poorly understood, particularly in rapidly urbanizing regions of eastern China. Here, we identified 211 macroinvertibrates species from 385 river sites in Ningbo, Zhejiang Province, China. We classified sites as low‐disturbance (LD) or high‐disturbance (HD) based on surrounding land use. This study examined differences in macroinvertebrate community composition, taxonomic and functional diversity, and functional feeding groups (FFGs) between disturbance levels, and further explored the potential direct and indirect effects of land use and environmental factors using structural equation modeling (SEM). Macroinvertebrate community composition differed significantly (p = 0.001) between LD and HD sites, with HD sites showing lower taxonomic and functional diversity. The relative abundance of FFGs also shifted with disturbance level, with filterers, gatherers, and predators more abundant at LD sites, whereas scrapers and shredders increased at HD sites. SEM further indicated that agricultural and urban land uses were negatively associated with both taxonomic and functional diversity, while non‐purgeable organic carbon (NPOC) showed a positive association with diversity. These findings demonstrate that anthropogenic land‐use disturbance can restructure macroinvertebrate communities and reduce multiple dimensions of biodiversity, highlighting the importance of integrating both taxonomic and functional information into ecological assessments of human‐dominated river systems.

articles.title: Fungus above us: exploring the atmospheric mycobiome by aircraft
paragraphs: Fungi play a key role in ecosystems, influencing the global bioaerosol budget and pollution dynamics even when metabolically inactive. Despite this, diversity and transport of fungi in the atmosphere are not well explored. This study shows that the atmosphere contains diverse fungi with varied ecological classifications and recruitment patterns reflecting underlying terrestrial habitats. Abundant genera include Neoascochyta, Cladosporium, Alternaria, Coniothyrium, Penicillium, Hymenochaetopsis, Lachnum, and Fonsecazyma. The atmospheric mycobiome is dominated by decomposers and pathogens; over 40% of the sampled airborne fungi are putative plant or animal pathogens. Using aircraft surveys from 2022 to 2023 in distinct seasons alongside comprehensive environmental datasets, airborne fungal diversity was found to decline with altitude and increasing vegetation productivity. Patterns of diversity in atmospheric fungal communities are shaped by vegetation productivity and meteorology. Remote sensing and meteorological data provide valuable insight into this diversity and reinforce the role of local or regional phenology as an important determinant of atmospheric biodiversity. Additionally, the proportional composition of functional guilds in the atmosphere shifts with vegetation productivity and surface winds, suggesting that seasonal transport dynamics may contribute to shaping assembly of the atmospheric mycobiome. This work demonstrates how integrated genomic and environmental datasets acquired by aircraft and satellite data could be leveraged in future to clarify aerobiology questions and contribute to a unified view of fungal ecology.

articles.title: Wolf Predation Likely Eliminated a Beaver Colony in a Drought‐Stressed Pond
paragraphs: Wolves and beavers increasingly co‐occur across the Northern Hemisphere, yet direct observations of their interactions remain rare, and little is known about how beavers respond behaviourally to predation risk under natural conditions. On 29 December 2024, a wolf killed an adult beaver on a foraging trail in Białowieża Forest, Poland, among the first video‐documented wolf–beaver predation events in Europe. Over the 53‐day monitoring period prior to the predation event, wolves visited the trail on 4 days, while beavers were active on 33 of those days (62%), averaging 4.9 detections per day (7.9 on days with activity). This contrasts with experimental work showing that predator cues alone are often enough to sharply suppress beaver activity. The predation occurred during hydrological drought. The watercourse above and below the pond was nearly dry, likely leaving the colony with nowhere safer to go. We interpret this apparent risk tolerance as consistent with the risk allocation hypothesis, where prey with no low‐risk foraging options cannot sustain antipredator behaviour without compromising essential foraging. Following the predation, the pond remained abandoned for at least 18 months. This expands on a previous report of ponds becoming inactive following wolves predating on dispersing beavers, suggesting predation can also displace established colonies, with potentially cascading consequences for water retention, nutrient cycling and vegetation dynamics. In drought‐affected landscapes, wolf predation could plausibly act as a spatial filter, disproportionately removing these ecosystem engineers from suboptimal habitats. This is a hypothesis that warrants future testing. As droughts intensify under climate change, this could compound into a feedback loop. Fewer active beaver sites would mean less landscape‐scale water retention, deepening drought and further constraining the beaver habitat that remains, and undermining the ecosystem functions that make beaver recolonisation so ecologically valuable.

articles.title: Regenerating forests around Taï National Park sustain biodiversity despite constrained floristic recovery
paragraphs: Extensive deforestation and disturbance have reshaped forest landscapes in West Africa, including areas surrounding Taï National Park, the largest remaining block of Upper Guinean rainforest. Although many degraded areas are currently undergoing regeneration, the capacity of these secondary forests to recover their biodiversity attributes remains insufficiently assessed within this park. This study quantifies the multidimensional restoration of biodiversity across 125 secondary forest plots and 15 primary forest plots representing 14,731 inventoried individuals in four sectors of the park. Using a Bayesian modelling framework, we estimate recovery trajectories of Shannon diversity, floristic composition, functional traits (wood density, leaf mass per area, seed mass), and conservation-relevant species. The different biodiversity attributes recovered at contrasting rates. Diversity was restored more rapidly (λ = 0.06) than floristic composition (λ = 0.03), and these recovery rates varied according to environmental variables. Among these, the presence of remnant trees showed the highest median on diversity (0.53 ± 0.61) and floristic composition (0.37 ± 0.17), promoting the rapid recovery of both attributes, followed by prior land use, particularly cocoa farming which also positively influenced the recovery of alpha diversity (λ = 0.03) and floristic composition (λ = 0.02). Regarding functional traits, they displayed contrasting dynamics: leaf mass per area (LMA) and seed mass recovered rapidly along successional gradients, whereas wood density followed a more gradual recovery trajectory. From a conservation perspective, although the proportion of IUCN Red List species remained stable along the successional gradient, old-growth indicator species were significantly more abundant in primary forests. To ensure the long-term conservation of biodiversity, protecting both primary and regenerating forests is essential to preserve the ecological resilience of this park.

articles.title: Weak dispersal and landscape size inevitably promote local biodiversity in heterogeneous metacommunities of competing species
paragraphs: We provide a general theoretical explanation for a longstanding result in spatial ecology: weak dispersal among habitat patches promotes local species richness. Using analytical approximations of spatial Lotka–Volterra competition models, we show that local species persistence in heterogeneous landscapes can be expressed as the balance between the total density across patches and the local exclusion rate. We further demonstrate that local multispecies coexistence is governed by the feasibility domain, linking spatial coexistence to a structural property of nonspatial competitive systems. Together, these results explain why weak dispersal increases local species richness and why this effect strengthens with the number of available patches, i.e., landscape size. We test these predictions using numerical simulations and find that the theory breaks down only when both dispersal and competitive interactions are very strong, in which case dispersal has a unimodal effect on coexistence. In contrast, landscape size retains a positive effect on coexistence whenever an effect is detectable. We then apply the theory to long-term data from a natural metacommunity of microcrustaceans. We detect strong competition among species and find no detectable effect of dispersal rate on local coexistence, whereas species co-occurrence increases with local landscape size, as predicted by theory. Together, our results identify how dispersal, interaction strength, and landscape size jointly regulate local species richness in competitive systems.

We study a long-standing question in ecology: why does a small amount of movement between habitats often increase the number of species that can live together locally? Although this pattern has been observed in many natural systems, a general explanation has been difficult to establish for communities containing many competing species. Using a mathematical model of species competition across connected habitats, we show that local coexistence depends on a simple balance between two forces. Species are more likely to persist in a habitat when they are abundant across the broader landscape and less likely to persist when strong competition would otherwise drive them locally extinct. This balance allows us to predict when dispersal among habitats promotes biodiversity and when it does not. We also show that the chance that all species coexist locally is closely linked to existing ecological theory developed for isolated communities. We test these predictions using computer simulations and long-term observations of microcrustaceans living in Finnish rock pools. We find strong agreement between theory and data, but also reveal the ecological situations in which it breaks down. Our results provide a unified framework linking dispersal, competition, landscape size, and biodiversity across spatially connected ecosystems.

articles.title: PoLoCo: a reproducible pooled low-coverage workflow for draft genome assembly and allele frequency analysis from ethanol-preserved small non-model invertebrates
paragraphs: Many ecologically important small invertebrates are preserved in ethanol, which compromises DNA integrity and severely limits their potential to be utilized in further genomic research. The lack of soil arthropod representation ultimately results in limited availability of reference genomes and population genomic inference from pooled sequencing (Pool-seq).

We introduce PoLoCo (Pooled Low-Coverage), a reproducible workflow integrating pooled specimen draft genome assembly from ethanol-preserved specimens with population-level allele-frequency analysis. We assembled a 411 Mb draft genome of Entomobrya nivalis from pooled short reads, achieving 97.7% BUSCO completeness despite notable fragmentation. Comparison with the published reference genome showed partial genomic correspondence while also revealing reference-dependent differences in the retained SNP datasets. The application of PoLoCo to 82 retained pooled populations produced a final distance-thinned allele-frequency dataset suitable for population-scale genomic inference. Case-study execution documented the computational requirements of the major workflow components on standard HPC infrastructure, with the workflow, documentation, and software environments openly available in Zenodo.

PoLoCo demonstrates that draft genome assemblies and reproducible Pool-seq allele-frequency analyses can be performed with long-preserved sample material from the field. PoLoCo integrates reference construction, sync-based allele-frequency analysis, and benchmarking into a free and open workflow. It establishes a reproducibility benchmark for biodiversity genomics and yields a transferable workflow for ecological and evolutionary initiatives where high-quality DNA or long-read sequencing is not feasible.

articles.title: An NB-IoT-Based Architecture with Spatial-Statistical Analytics for Cross-Domain Air and Water Quality Monitoring in Aquaculture and Aquatic Environments
paragraphs: The rapid expansion of smart agriculture and precision aquaculture necessitates continuous, high-resolution environmental monitoring to optimize ecosystem stability and prevent catastrophic biomass loss. Conventional Internet of Things (IoT) solutions routinely treat atmospheric and aquatic parameters as isolated domains, neglecting the dynamic physicochemical coupling occurring across the air–water boundary layer. To overcome this domain fragmentation, this study presents an integrated edge-cloud telemetry architecture designed for concurrent, multi-domain environmental monitoring and cross-domain spatial-statistical analysis. The proposed framework employs low-cost, multi-sensor edge nodes integrated with Narrowband IoT (NB-IoT) cellular communication, achieving high signal penetration, energy-efficient operation, and direct base-station connectivity without local gateway dependencies. The system continuously acquires atmospheric parameters (temperature, relative humidity, particulate matter PM1.0/PM2.5/PM10, ozone O3, total volatile organic compounds TVOC, equivalent CO2, Air Quality Index AQI, and Ultraviolet Index UVI) alongside aquatic indicators (water temperature, pH, dissolved oxygen DO, electrical conductivity EC, and turbidity). Telemetry is streamed via Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) to a centralized MySQL cloud database, providing real-time Grafana dashboards, spatial Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) mapping, and automated multi-channel alerting via LINE Notify and email. The architecture was deployed and validated across the Tunghai University aquatic research facility, capturing n = 14,400 synchronized 1-min observations (with an initial raw Packet Delivery Rate of 99.24%). Statistical evaluations accounting for temporal autocorrelation (Neff≈892) and False Discovery Rate correction revealed significant cross-domain associations (padj<0.001), notably an inverse association (r=−0.782, ρ=−0.794, τ=−0.612) between ambient air temperature and aquatic dissolved oxygen physically consistent with Henry’s Law of gas solubility, an inverse association (r=−0.763) between atmospheric humidity and dissolved oxygen, and a positive association (r=+0.789, ρ=+0.812) between humidity and aquatic turbidity. First-order partial correlation analysis (rTa,DO∣Tw=−0.172) confirmed that water temperature serves as the primary thermal mediator of dissolved oxygen depletion. By synergizing low-power NB-IoT telemetry with robust multi-domain analytics, this work provides a scalable, empirical foundation for transitioning from reactive threshold alerting to proactive predictive management in precision aquaculture.

articles.title: Cave‐Dwelling Planariidae in Dinaric Karst Exhibit Differing Levels of Cave Trait Evolution
paragraphs: The Dinaric karst encompasses a network of over 10,000 caves and represents one of the world's most important subterranean biodiversity hotspots. It is inhabited by remarkably diverse and often endemic species, including planarian flatworms. Although cave planarians have long been known from the region, they have not yet been investigated using an integrative approach, and their evolutionary relationships with surface‐dwelling relatives remain unresolved. To address these gaps, we combined field sampling, phylogenetic analyses based on the COI and 18S genes, and phenotypic characterisation. Our results show that cave planariids in the Dinaric karst belong to at least three genera and are more widespread and diverse than previously assumed. We increased the number of cave records in the Dinaric karst from 26 to 37 and documented cf. Atrioplanaria and Phagocata in Croatian caves for the first time. Phylogenetic reconstructions are consistent with independent cave colonisation events, including multiple instances within the genera Crenobia and cf. Atrioplanaria. Variation in pigmentation and eye reduction, both within and between populations, further reveals heterogeneous evolutionary trajectories of cave‐associated phenotypes. Our molecular phylogeny and documentation of trait variability constitute a first step towards establishing Planariidae as a model for investigating the mechanisms underlying the convergent evolution of pigment loss and eye reduction in cave environments.

articles.title: Ecosystem Health Assessment of Hulun Lake Using an eDNA Metabarcoding‐Based Phytoplankton Index of Biotic Integrity
paragraphs: Hulun Lake, one of the largest freshwater lakes in China, is currently experiencing significant water quality deterioration. Therefore, water quality assessment is of paramount importance, as it not only provides critical insights into the current pollution status of lakes but also offers a scientific basis for effective lake management and ecological restoration. Using environmental DNA‐metabarcoding data from 13 sampling sites in Hulun Lake in June 2023, our study explored the spatial variation of α‐diversity, the community composition, and phytoplankton index of biotic integrity (P‐IBI). A total of 431 phytoplankton species were identified across 10 phyla, 191 families, and 335 genera, with Chlorophyta and Bacillariophyta predominating. Biodiversity was higher in the northern and southern regions, except for the site XHK, but lower in the central region. P‐IBI scores exhibited clear spatial variation, with relatively high scores in the central and northern regions, except for the site XHK, indicating comparatively favorable ecological conditions. In contrast, lower P‐IBI scores were observed in the southern region, except for DNHWZ and GZ, suggesting relatively greater ecological degradation. The P‐IBI scores were significantly negatively correlated with Water Quality Index (WQI) values, indicating that higher biotic integrity was generally associated with better physicochemical water quality. RDA and Spearman rank correlation analyses revealed that ammonia nitrogen (NH3–N) and total organic carbon (TOC) were positively correlated with P‐IBI, whereas temperature (T) and total nitrogen (TN) showed negative correlations with P‐IBI, indicating that spatial variation in P‐IBI was closely associated with nutrient status and organic carbon availability. Lake management should integrate both P‐IBI and WQI‐based assessment approaches, providing a scientifically robust basis for the identification of environmental pressures and the diagnosis of ecological health.

articles.title: Geographic variation in Dendrocalamus latiflorus culm physical and mechanical traits is associated with source-climate gradients
paragraphs: Geographic variation in bamboo culm traits can reveal associations between source environments and biomechanical performance and can help prioritize germplasm for further testing.

We quantified 11 physical and mechanical traits in 31 geographic sources of Dendrocalamus latiflorus from nine provincial-level regions of China and related source-level means to 25 geographic and climatic variables. Analyses combined coefficients of variation, Pearson correlations with Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction, partial least squares regression (PLSR) with leave-one-out cross-validation and 1,000 bootstrap resamples, Moran’s I tests of residual spatial autocorrelation, principal component analysis, objectively validated Ward clustering, and a seven-trait entropy-weighted TOPSIS evaluation with equal-weight sensitivity analysis.

Trait coefficients of variation ranged from 7.1% to 24.4%. After correction of 100 Pearson tests, 32 associations remained significant at q < 0.05; the strongest was between precipitation of the warmest quarter (BIO18) and compressive strength parallel to grain (CSPG; r = 0.658, q = 0.0058). PLSR showed the highest cross-validated performance for CSPG (Q2 = 0.599), moderate performance for air-dry and oven-dry density, and weak performance for modulus of rupture (Q2 = 0.076). Raw density and CSPG values were spatially autocorrelated, but PLSR residuals were not. Two validated trait classes showed no significant differences in six key source-climate variables. Entropy-weighted TOPSIS ranked P6, P4, and P19 highest; equal weighting produced strongly concordant ranks (Spearman rho = 0.911).
These results identify robust climate-associated trait patterns and candidate sources for further testing while avoiding causal inference from source-site sampling.

articles.title: The agricultural synergistic dividend of environmental regulation and the identification of the net total effect: Evidence from China’s Air Pollution Prevention and Control Action Plan
paragraphs: This study evaluates the agricultural co-benefits of large-scale environmental regulation. Existing studies often focus on crop yields and condition on production inputs that may themselves respond to policy interventions, potentially understating the overall production effect. Using Chinese county-level panel data from 2000 to 2024, we employ a reduced-form difference-in-differences (DiD) design to estimate the net total effect of the Air Pollution Prevention and Control Action Plan (hereafter, the Action Plan) on per-capita agricultural output, with double machine learning used as a robustness check for flexible meteorological adjustment. The baseline DiD estimates indicate that the policy increased per-capita output of grain, vegetables and edible fungi, and oilseeds by approximately 42.6%, 10.4%, and 18.1%, respectively, in key regulated regions. Mechanism analysis shows that the policy significantly reduced fine particulate matter (PM2.5) concentrations, consistent with the proposed biophysical pathway linking improved air quality to agricultural production. The reduced-form design may also retain production adjustments induced by environmental improvement, although these behavioral responses are not directly identified. Heterogeneity analysis indicates stronger grain responses in northern regions, whereas vegetables, edible fungi, and oilseeds show stronger responses in the South; grain and oilseed responses are also stronger in high-population areas. These findings provide evidence of agricultural co-benefits from air-pollution regulation and support closer coordination between environmental and agricultural policies.

articles.title: Inverter control for wind–solar–storage based on distributed generation and virtual synchronous machines
paragraphs: To enhance the operational stability of the power system and address the issues of weak inertia support and sluggish dynamic response of traditional inverter control strategies when dealing with complex scenarios involving a high proportion of new energy sources, a new intelligent control strategy has been proposed. This study adopts the VSG control strategy as the core technology for the regulation of wind-solar-storage power generation inverters, and divides the dynamic response process into acceleration period, deceleration period, reverse acceleration period and reverse deceleration period. Different control strategies are adopted for different system states at different stages. Additionally, the DDPG algorithm is introduced, and the single DDPG agent is extended to a multi-agent interactive deep deterministic policy gradient algorithm. Finally, the multi-agent collaborative optimization is achieved in a “centralized training and decentralized execution” form. The research results show that in the case of sudden load increase, the voltage deviation at the grid connection point is stabilized at 371.7 V, and the voltage recovery time is significantly shorter than the comparison strategy. At the same time, the time-weighted absolute error integral reaches optimal values of 1.82 V/s2 and 1.85 V/s2 in scenarios of sudden load increase and sudden drops in photovoltaic power, and the strategy efficiency reaches 97.83%, and the steady-state accuracy reaches 99.63%, demonstrating superior control capabilities. In the three typical fault conditions of practical application, the average frequency deviation of the control strategy was 0.197 Hz, the number of protection lockouts was 0.3 times, the average depth of voltage sag was 24.63%, the average recovery time was 1.21 hours, and the number of abnormal warnings did not exceed 5 times. The proposed framework for coordinated wind, solar, and storage regulation, based on distributed power generation and virtual synchronous machine, can effectively support the safe, flexible, and efficient operation of the new power system under high penetration of renewable energy.

articles.title: Quantifying Light-Absorbing Aerosol Snow Darkening Using Cryogenic Snow Generation and Integrating Sphere Spectrophotometry
paragraphs: The deposition of light-absorbing aerosols like dark brown carbon (d-BrC) accelerates cryospheric melt, yet accurately modeling this radiative forcing is hindered by a lack of empirical data. To address this gap, we developed a novel, low-footprint laboratory snow synthesis and deposition apparatus. This system couples the cryogenic generation of synthetic snow with controlled aerosol dry deposition, allowing spectral albedo reductions to be quantified via an integrating sphere spectrophotometer. The setup was rigorously validated using Cabojet, a highly absorbing black carbon (BC) proxy, achieving high-fidelity optical closure with the Snow, Ice, and Aerosol Radiative (SNICAR) model (root-mean-square error < 0.022) and establishing a 165 parts per billion (ppb) detection limit of BC in snow. Applying this validated methodology to nebulized d-BrC tarballs revealed that the dry deposition of ∼1000 ppb d-BrC drives a visible broadband albedo decrease of 0.06. This apparatus offers a highly controlled, empirical platform to ground-truth theoretical radiative forcing calculations for diverse, real-world cryospheric contaminants. Further, by introducing a modular and rapid laboratory setup, these experiments overcome the limitations of outdoor field studies and resource-intensive cold rooms.

articles.title: Environmental Cancer Risk Scenarios for Lebanon: Quantitative Sensitivity Analysis and a Qualitative Genetic Susceptibility Framework
paragraphs: Background: Environmental exposures and biological susceptibility contribute to the complexity in cancer vulnerability, particularly in settings where comprehensive environmental monitoring and longitudinal exposure data are limited. Scenario-based modeling can provide a structured approach for exploring potential environmental cancer risks under uncertainty and identifying priorities for future research and surveillance. Methods: We developed a scenario-based environmental cancer risk framework for Lebanon incorporating three exposure domains—perchlorate contamination, nitrate/nitrite exposure, and conflict-derived environmental contamination— and a qualitative Genetic Susceptibility Index (GSI). Monte Carlo simulations with 100,000 iterations were used to propagate uncertainty in literature-derived epidemiological effect estimates for colorectal and lung cancers under alternative hypothetical scaling assumptions. The GSI was used to organize qualitative susceptibility pathways but was not incorporated as a numerical modifier in the simulations. Thyroid cancer was evaluated separately through an illustrative hypothetical sensitivity analysis using author-defined relative-effect ranges because direct epidemiological estimates linking perchlorate exposure to thyroid cancer incidence were unavailable. Results: For colorectal cancer, the mean simulated relative effect increased from 3.79% (95% UI: 1.90–5.70%) under the low-exposure-contrast scenario to 7.72% (95% UI: 3.83–11.71%) under the moderate scenario and 16.09% (95% UI: 7.81–24.80%) under the high scenario, which applied the full published log-relative effect. For lung cancer, corresponding mean simulated relative effects were 2.18% (95% UI: 1.01–3.36%), 4.41% (95% UI: 2.02–6.83%), and 9.03% (95% UI: 4.09–14.13%). Under the full published exposure contrast, 92.34% of colorectal cancer simulations exceeded a 10% relative-effect threshold and 94.52% of lung cancer simulations exceeded a 5% threshold. The thyroid cancer analysis produced mean simulated relative effects of 1.03%, 3.50%, and 7.51% under the low-, moderate-, and high-scenario assumptions, respectively; these outputs were conditional on the prespecified hypothetical ranges. Conclusions: This framework demonstrates how alternative exposure-contrast assumptions can influence the distribution of literature-derived relative effects in a data-limited setting. By combining quantitative exposure-contrast sensitivity analysis with a qualitative genetic susceptibility framework, the approach may support environmental health planning, surveillance prioritization, and the design of future population-based studies in Lebanon. The thyroid cancer results illustrate model behavior under author-defined hypothetical assumptions and do not constitute epidemiological estimates of perchlorate-associated thyroid cancer risk. articles.title: The Environmental Exposome and Age-Related Macular Degeneration: Oxidative Stress as a Molecular Link
paragraphs: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is a multifactorial retinal disease in which genetic susceptibility, aging, metabolic dysfunction, and environmental factors interact to determine disease onset and progression. Although environmental exposures are increasingly recognized as modifiable risk factors for AMD, the molecular mechanisms linking cumulative environmental stress to retinal degeneration remain incompletely understood. In this review, we examine the environmental exposome relevant to AMD and propose oxidative stress as a central molecular link connecting diverse environmental exposures with retinal aging and AMD susceptibility. Epidemiological evidence linking air pollution, particulate matter, cigarette smoke, and other environmental stressors to AMD is reviewed, followed by an analysis of their effects on redox homeostasis and the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)–Bruch’s membrane–choriocapillaris complex. We further discuss how chronic oxidative stress promotes mitochondrial dysfunction, lipid peroxidation, ferroptosis, autophagy and mitophagy impairment, cellular senescence, and senescence-associated inflammation. These processes interact with complement activation, microglial activation, and chronic retinal inflammation, ultimately contributing to RPE dysfunction, choriocapillaris and Bruch’s membrane abnormalities, photoreceptor degeneration, and AMD progression. Integrating these mechanisms, we propose an environmental exposome–oxidative stress–retinal aging axis in which cumulative environmental exposures progressively reduce retinal resilience and increase susceptibility to AMD. We also evaluate antioxidant and redox-modulating strategies, including the established evidence for AREDS/AREDS2 supplementation and emerging approaches targeting Nrf2 signaling, glutathione homeostasis, mitochondria, and ferroptosis. Importantly, antioxidant supplementation should not be equated with primary prevention of environmentally induced AMD. Future studies integrating individual exposure monitoring, oxidative stress biomarkers, genetic susceptibility, and retinal phenotyping may enable precision prevention and personalized redox-based interventions. This framework positions environmental exposure as a potentially modifiable driver of retinal biological aging and provides a mechanistic basis for understanding and preventing environmentally driven AMD.

articles.title: Multicentre Evaluation of Loop-Mediated Isothermal Amplification (LAMP) for Environmental Monitoring of Nosocomial Pathogens in Italian Hospitals
paragraphs: Background: Environmental contamination of hospital surfaces, especially in high-risk clinical areas, partly sustains healthcare-associated infections. The detection of microbiological contamination in hospital settings using culture-based methods remains fundamental, even though these methods are not rapid, show moderate sensitivity in areas with low microbial loads, and are unsuitable for some microbial species. This multicentre study evaluated the performance of loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) for the rapid detection of major nosocomial pathogens on hospital surfaces. Methods: A multicentre observational method–comparison study was conducted in three Italian hospital centres. Overall, 298 environmental surface samples were collected from clinical areas included in local infection-prevention monitoring plans. For each sampling point, LAMP swab sampling was paired with an adjacent contact plate culture. LAMP assays targeted Staphylococcus aureus, Acinetobacter baumannii, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Manual and automated nucleic acid extraction workflows were analysed separately. Diagnostic performance, agreement metrics, and discordant paired results were assessed using a contact plate culture as the microbiological comparator. Results: No LAMP-negative/RODAC-positive pairs were observed. Positive percent agreement (PPA) relative to contact plate culture was therefore 100% in the subgroups evaluated. Relative specificity ranged from 90.9% to 98.6%, while overall accuracy ranged from 93.8% to 98.6%. Discordant results were exclusively LAMP-positive/contact plate-negative and were more frequent for S. aureus and P. aeruginosa. Selective culture verification supported several LAMP-positive findings not recovered by routine contact plates. Conclusions: LAMP showed high negative agreement, high specificity, and rapid target-specific detection of selected nosocomial pathogens on hospital surfaces. It may complement conventional cultures in environmental surveillance, particularly when timely feedback is needed to guide infection-prevention and sanitation-monitoring strategies.

articles.title: Atopic Dermatitis in the Era of Exposome and Artificial Intelligence
paragraphs: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a heterogeneous, relapsing inflammatory skin disease in which epidermal barrier dysfunction, immune dysregulation, microbial imbalance, genetics, and the environment interact continuously over time. Although a substantial body of literature has linked AD with air pollution, weather, allergens, stress, infections, sleep disturbance, skin care practices and microbial perturbation, most studies have assessed single exposures in isolation. This reductionist approach only partially reflects the real-world biology of AD, where patients experience dynamic combinations of external and internal exposures whose effects are non-linear, cumulative and modified by age, phenotype, treatment and susceptibility. The exposome paradigm offers a broader conceptual lens by considering the totality of exposures over the life course. However, exposomic research in AD is methodologically challenging because the data are multimodal, high-dimensional, time-dependent, and often incomplete. Artificial intelligence (AI) can help address this complexity by integrating heterogeneous data layers, modelling temporal dependencies, discovering latent patterns, and generating individualized predictions. This narrative review examines current evidence and proposes a theoretical framework that integrates AI and the exposome in AD. We define the principal domains of the AD exposome, describe a multilevel analytical architecture spanning environmental, clinical, behavioural, microbiome, and multi-omics data. We distinguish applications evaluated in AD studies from exploratory analyses and proposed objectives: prediction of annual flare burden remains exploratory, whereas exposome-informed short-term flare alerts are proposed applications. Although selected AI applications have been evaluated in AD, the added predictive value of exposure data and the clinical utility of a fully integrated exposome–AI system remain to be established. We also outline key methodological and translational priorities, including exposure assessment, temporality, treatment-confounding, interpretability, fairness, data governance, and external validation. The proposed framework offers a structured basis for future research, with clinical translation dependent on prospective validation and evidence of benefit to patient care.

articles.title: Intelligence-enabled smart inhalable biomaterials for chronic inflammatory airway diseases: integrating responsive carrier engineering, lung-on-chip validation, and patient-specific pulmonary modeling
paragraphs: Chronic inflammatory airway diseases, particularly asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), are commonly treated by inhalation, yet the nominal dose placed in an inhaler often differs substantially from the dose that reaches diseased airway regions, crosses mucus, enters target cells, and remains pharmacologically active. Airway narrowing, heterogeneous ventilation, mucus plugging, impaired mucociliary clearance, oxidative and proteolytic stress, epithelial barrier dysfunction, inflammatory-cell diversity, device characteristics, and patient-specific inhalation maneuvers jointly shape therapeutic exposure. Smart inhalable biomaterials can be designed to address some of these barriers by controlling transport, retention, activation, or release, but many systems are still optimized primarily at the nanoparticle level and evaluated in static models that do not capture realistic aerosol performance or patient-specific deposition. This review develops an intelligence-enabled bioengineering framework linking disease-informed material design with machine-learning-assisted formulation optimization, formulation–device–patient coupling, lung-on-chip validation, and patient-specific pulmonary modeling. Within this framework, airway features such as mucus architecture, redox gradients, protease activity, epithelial permeability, immune-cell state, extracellular-matrix remodeling, and regional airflow are considered measurable variables that can inform material design and evaluation. The material platforms considered include mucus-penetrating and mucoadhesive carriers, responsive materials, transformable nano-in-micro systems, polymeric and lipid nanoparticles, biomimetic carriers, extracellular vesicles, and systems for pulmonary delivery of nucleic acids and biologics. Their development is considered alongside structured experimental design, machine learning, active learning, mechanistic aerosol modeling, physics-informed surrogates, multi-objective optimization, and uncertainty analysis. Lung-on-chip systems provide human-relevant settings in which deposited dose, mucus transport, barrier function, immune responses, and repeated-exposure effects can be examined under air–liquid-interface and breathing-like conditions. Patient-specific computational fluid dynamics and reduced-order models can complement these platforms by predicting regional deposition, whereas the term digital twin should be reserved for longitudinally updated, uncertainty-aware models linked to actionable decisions. Together, these approaches support a closed-loop design–delivery–validation strategy in which material performance, aerosol behavior, biological response, and patient-specific deposition are evaluated as connected rather than separate development problems.

articles.title: Sustainability and Integrated Energy Recovery Scheme for Health Care Waste Management for Megacity Dhaka: Through Material Flow and Life Cycle Assessment
paragraphs: A sustainable healthcare waste (HCW) management strategy for Dhaka integrating material flow analysis and comparative life cycle assessment is proposed. The current scenario (SC1), heavily reliant on landfilling, low recycling, and incineration without energy integration, is compared with the proposed alternative scenario (SC2), with higher material recycling, waste‐to‐energy conversion, and heat integration. Using gate‐to‐grave life‐cycle assessment across eighteen ReCiPe 2016 midpoint (H) impact categories, the proposed SC2 outperforms SC1 in ten categories, notably acidification potential by 96%, land‐use potential by 97%, climate change impacts by 78%, and marine eutrophication by 44%, while PM formation potential falls by 20.499 kg PM2.5‐eq and energy resource depletion becomes a net credit through 20572 kWh/day of recovered electricity. However, trade‐offs are observed in the toxicity, eutrophication, and photochemical oxidant formation categories, notably carcinogenic human toxicity (∼3.8x increase), marine ecotoxicity (∼2.3x increase), freshwater eutrophication (∼97% increase), and photochemical oxidant formation potential (∼3x increase). The proposed scheme also supports Bangladesh's drive toward SDG 7 and 13 outright, and toward SDG 3, 6, 11, and 14 once the toxicity and oxidant formation burdens are controlled. Our findings can provide a substantial quantitative framework for improving existing systems to achieve sustainability with a circular economy strategy.

articles.title: An integrated multi-scale framework for economically feasible landscape connectivity in working agricultural systems
paragraphs: Agricultural landscapes must simultaneously sustain food production, support rural economies, and maintain ecological resilience. However, decades of landscape simplification have reduced semi-natural habitats, fragmented ecological networks, and weakened the ecosystem services that underpin agricultural productivity. Existing approaches to ecological intensification improve some farm-level services but do not generate the spatial coordination required for landscape-scale ecological function. Here, we present an integrated modeling framework that links farm-level ecological intensification, spatial habitat connectivity optimization, and a Bayesian search over realistic agri-environmental policies. Applied to a real agricultural landscape, the framework identifies feasible pathways for enhancing ecological function while maintaining economic viability. By explicitly connecting the scales at which farmers make decisions, ecosystems operate, and policies are implemented, this approach reveals how coordinated restoration can transform fragmented agricultural mosaics into more resilient, multifunctional landscapes. Our results demonstrate the potential for policy design to enable ecologically strategic and economically feasible habitat restoration, offering a pathway toward more sustainable agricultural systems.

articles.title: PhenoFECT: A Python package for forecasting and exploring plant phenology under climate change
paragraphs: Climate change and global warming significantly affect the timing of plant flowering in spring. Accurately predicting these phenological events is crucial for understanding plant biology and agriculture. The chill‐day model (CDM) based on seasonal temperature changes has been a reliable model for predicting phenological activities; however, recent global warming has challenged its accuracy due to extreme weather variability, necessitating the adjustment of the CDM parameters to reflect recent climate change. We developed an open‐source Python package, PhenoFECT (Phenology Forecasting Exploring ClimaTe), that refines temperature‐based phenology models. The package enables efficient phenological analysis for open and user‐specified data.

The Python package embeds open meteorological data collected over 53 years (1973–2025) in Korea for cherry (Prunus yedoensis), golden‐bell (Forsythia koreana), and azalea (Rhododendron mucronulatum). PhenoFECT was utilized to adjust the parameters of the CDM to reflect recent climate changes. The refined CDM improved the prediction accuracy of flowering at the average root mean square error (RMSE) of 5.74 days for three angiosperms.

PhenoFECT is a versatile tool for accurate forecasting, exploration, and visualization across diverse open meteorological data. Exploring data using PhenoFECT revealed that the CDM can be influenced by geographic features and global climate phenomena.

articles.title: Contact in context: How land use histories, sociocultural practices, and animal profiles shape human-animal contact and zoonotic pathogen exposure in a fragmented forest of the Democratic Republic of Congo
paragraphs: Pathogenic spillovers from animals into humans have catalyzed epidemics throughout history. They result from multiple factors. articles.title: The role of ponds in the retention of micro(nano)plastics, tyre wear particles and their leachates: current state of the science, research gaps and opportunities
paragraphs: Natural and artificial ponds offer a cost-effective management technique to potentially remove water contaminants including micro(nano)plastics (MNPs) and tyre wear particles (TWPs). The use of sustainable urban drainage systems (SuDS), including ponds, is increasingly being promoted by governmental guidance in countries such as the UK, the USA, and Denmark in part to address contaminated runoff in new road and housing developments with increasing calls to make these systems mandatory. Traditionally, the focus has been on the removal of contaminants such as metals, suspended particles, PAHs and pesticides, improving water quality and reducing diffuse pollution. In more recent years, the efficacy of ponds in the removal of MPs and TWPs has been increasingly investigated. Studies estimate, albeit with potentially substantial uncertainty, that pond removal efficiencies for microplastics (MPs) and TWPs range from 83.9% to 99.9% and 80.1% to 100.0%, respectively. However, with current legislative steps toward ponds becoming increasingly widespread as a remediation tool, there are a number of significant gaps in the current body of research that need to be addressed. The transport and fate of nanoplastics (NPs) need to be examined, TWPs need to be consistently included in studies, and the transport through ponds of contaminants sorbed by MNPs and TWPs alongside manufacturing additives leached by MNPs and TWPs must be considered. As analytical techniques develop and are standardised, future studies should ensure that these aspects are considered more thoroughly to enable relevant conclusions to be drawn that could shape the design of future pond systems.

articles.title: The microbial aerial thread: co-restoring source and sink across dryland-urban gradients
paragraphs: Dryland ecosystems serve as major sources of atmospheric bioaerosols through aeolian transport of dust-associated microorganisms. These microbial communities are dispersed across vast distances, connecting dryland soils and vegetation to distant recipient ecosystems, particularly urban areas. This review synthesizes current understanding of microbial ecology in arid soils, microbial dispersal through dust, and interactions with urban ecosystems. We propose that restoration efforts should move beyond isolated, site-level interventions toward integrated strategies that account for the atmospheric connectivity between dryland source areas and urban sink environments. Practical restoration approaches, including dryland soil stabilization to reduce harmful dust emissions, microbial inoculant development, and urban green infrastructure designed to function as dispersal corridors, can generate cross-boundary synergies that enhance ecological resilience across the dryland–urban gradient. By reconceptualizing cities as nodes within broader ecological networks linked by microbial dispersal, and by leveraging insights from dryland ecology to guide urban restoration under resource-limited conditions, this framework offers a pathway for co-restoring connected landscapes in an era of accelerating urbanization and desertification.

articles.title: Adaptive Mechanisms of Endemic Fish Triplophysa yarkandensis in the Tarim River Basin of Northwestern China
paragraphs: Freshwater fish living in dryland rivers face increasing threats from climate change, water shortages, increasing salt levels, habitat changes, and human activities. These challenges are especially serious for native fish species that survive only in limited areas. This study reviewed how the endemic fish Triplophysa yarkandensis adapts to the harsh environment of the Tarim River Basin and identified the factors affecting its survival. The review highlights key responses of T. yarkandensis, including osmoregulatory mechanisms that maintain ion balance under saline–alkaline stress, activation of the IRE1–JNK signaling axis associated with heat-stress-induced apoptosis, and the functional roles of the gut microbiota in metabolism, nutrient utilization, and stress resilience. The review also highlighted how changes in water availability, habitat loss, pollution, and introduced species may reduce its ability to survive in the future. Understanding these survival strategies provides important knowledge for protecting native fish populations and maintaining healthy freshwater ecosystems. The findings can support better conservation planning, habitat restoration, and management strategies to protect aquatic biodiversity in dryland river systems under future environmental changes.

Dryland river ecosystems are among the most susceptible freshwater environments, with climate change, hydrological shifts, salinization and anthropogenic disturbance posing increasing threats to aquatic biodiversity. Endemic fishes in these regions are particularly vulnerable because of restricted geographic range, ecological specialization and narrow environmental tolerance limits, which reduce their capacity to cope with rapid environmental change. Triplophysa yarkandensis has a coordinated set of adaptive responses such as benthic morphological specialization, adaptable trophic modes, osmoregulatory ability to cope with saline–alkaline stress, and thermal tolerance mediated by stress-sensitive genes. Notably, muscle transcriptomic evidence indicates heat-associated expression changes in genes of the IRE1–TRAF2–MAP3K5–JNK signaling axis, suggesting this pathway as a candidate link between endoplasmic-reticulum stress and apoptosis-related responses. But its activation and causal role in apoptosis have not yet been confirmed at the protein and functional level. Nevertheless, these adaptations are increasingly constrained by habitat fragmentation, invasive species, declining water quality, and altered flow regimes, highlighting the limited buffering capacity of endemic species under increasing environmental disturbance. These observations provide a scientific basis for conservation planning, ecological monitoring, and adaptive management in arid inland waters, including habitat restoration, ecological flow regulation, and species-specific protection. Future studies must combine long-term field studies, multi-stressor experimental systems, and genomic–ecophysiological designs to define adaptive limits and improve conservation outcomes under continued climate change.

articles.title: Eco-Virological Patterns of Zoonotic Viruses in Neotropical Bats: Insights for Host Species Distributed in the Northern Andes—A Scoping Review and Trait-Based Analysis
paragraphs: Bats are recognized as important reservoirs of zoonotic viruses; however, the ecological determinants shaping virus–host associations in regions of high biodiversity remain poorly understood. In this study, we conducted a scoping review and a trait-based analysis to characterize eco-virological patterns of zoonotic RNA viruses reported in Neotropical bat species whose distributions include the Northern Andes (Colombia, Ecuador, and Venezuela). We compiled 578 unique viral detection records reported across Neotropics from 235 studies and sequence records for 56 bat species occurring in the Northern Andes, including members of the families Coronaviridae, Flaviviridae, Orthomyxoviridae, Paramyxoviridae, and Rhabdoviridae. Ecological, spatial, and life-history traits of host species were incorporated, and their associations were evaluated using multiple correspondence analysis, chi-square tests, and Cramér’s V statistics. Although multivariate analyses and flow diagrams suggested recurrent ecological patterns, statistical tests revealed weak and non-significant associations between viral families and ecological traits (V = 0.05–0.20; p > 0.05). Viral records were concentrated in lowland, non-migratory species with generalist roosting behavior and frequent use of anthropogenic habitats; however, these patterns likely reflect host availability and sampling effort rather than ecological specialization. Viral detections were distributed across multiple ecological contexts, suggesting broad virus–host associations among Neotropical bat species. Importantly, we identified a marked geographical bias in the available evidence: 64.0% of records originated from Brazil, whereas direct records from the Northern Andes were scarce (Colombia: 5.0%) or absent (Ecuador and Venezuela: 0%). Consequently, our findings provide a baseline of potential viral diversity and virus–host associations for bat species occurring in the Northern Andes rather than direct evidence of local viral circulation. These results highlight critical knowledge gaps and underscore the need for strengthened surveillance and One Health research across the Northern Andes.

articles.title: Grazing Management Regimen Shapes Soil Carbon Stocks and Associated Bacterial Community Composition in a Semi-Arid Rangeland
paragraphs: Drylands and natural grasslands are increasingly threatened by overgrazing and climate change, which damage soil functionality and reduce their natural carbon sequestration capacity. This study evaluated how different livestock management practices, such as high-stocking-density rotational grazing and temporary rest periods, relate to soil carbon storage and bacterial community structures. The findings suggest that non-selective intensive grazing is associated with higher soil carbon levels and distinct microbial groups linked to potential nutrient cycling and organic matter turnover. In contrast, long-term rest and fencing tend to favor more stable carbon forms. Ultimately, these exploratory results provide preliminary evidence that well-managed non-selective intensive grazing livestock practices may contribute to potential soil carbon storage and microbial community adjustments, supporting future restoration efforts in semi-arid rangelands.

Semi-arid rangelands are highly vulnerable to climate change and overgrazing, yet the functional coupling between soil carbon stabilization and microbial recovery remains largely unquantified. This study was carried out in Northern Mexico (24°0′33″ N, 104°42′28″ W, 1990 m.a.s.l.) and evaluated associations between a grazing management gradient comprising continuous grazing (CG), closed non-selective intensive grazing (GE), and open non-selective intensive grazing (SG) on soil carbon stocks and different labile fractions, bacterial community structures, and functional metabolic pathways in semi-arid soils. The results show that SG showed the highest observed organic and inorganic carbon stocks (SOC and SIC stocks, respectively), along with the labile carbon (LC) fraction. Conversely, GE favors the accumulation of stable, non-labile carbon (NLC). Although alpha diversity remained unaffected, grazing management induced differences in beta diversity. Redundancy and LEfSe analyses revealed a strong coupling between carbon fractions and microbial assembly, characterized by the exclusive enrichment of copiotrophic biomarker families (Burkholderiaceae and Sphingobacteriaceae) under SG. Furthermore, predictive functional profiling (PICRUSt2 and ANCOM) showed that pathways such as tRNA charging and nicotinate degradation were enriched under SG and GE, reflecting potential metabolic capacities and inferred microbial adjustments to heterogeneous, excreta-derived nutrient microenvironments during intermediate recovery states. Ultimately, the findings suggest that targeted rotational grazing may contribute to improved soil carbon stocks and microbial community recovery in semi-arid rangelands.
